title: How the Chinese Communist Party Stays in Power
transcriptText:
China [music] is one of the 21st
century's most consequential nations. It
has never been more important to
understand how the country [music] is
governed and what its leaders and its
people actually want and believe.
Welcome to Pekingology,
>> [music]
>> the podcast that unpacks China's
evolving political system and the
trajectory of China's domestic and
foreign policy. I'm your host, Henrietta
Levin, senior fellow with the Freeman
Chair in China Studies at CSIS. [music]
This is Pekingology.
I am so pleased to be joined today by
Ben Hillman, director of the Australian
Centre on China in the world at
Australian National University and
co-editor of a fantastic new book, The
Communist Party of China,
Understanding the durability of the
world's most powerful political
organization.
This volume tackles the question of why
and how the CCP, the world's second
longest ruling party anywhere, has been
so successful at maintaining its own
power.
And the party's durability, I think is
all the more impressive when we think
about the almost incomprehensible scale
of change in China's economy and society
since 1945. And yet here the party is
maintaining a strong on on power through
that whole duration and through a very
significant period of change. And so I'm
really glad Ben is here to unpack the
CCP's rather remarkable staying power.
So, Ben, thank you so much for coming on
the show. Thanks, Henrietta. It's a
pleasure to be here and to be talking
about our new book, which I co-edited
with my ANU colleague Feng Yuanji, and
which is the culmination of many years'
work by scholars in Australia and around
the world. Well, we like to start all of
our episodes with a question about how
our guest developed their interest in
China and their expertise. So, what did
that look like for you?
Well, I first went to China in the early
'90s and I spent time in the northeast,
in Jilin province, studying Chinese
initially.
And I was really struck at the time by
the pace of change, the effervescent
entrepreneurialism,
and people's appetite for new ideas.
In the northeast, which was a
development laggard, I got insights into
how people lived in Mao's era.
The people still lived in their work
units and the friendship store was the
only place to buy anything you needed.
My teachers were retired literature
professors who told me stories about
life under Mao and the changes they'd
witnessed. And I really wanted to learn
more. So, after finishing my bachelor's
degree, I went back to China, this time
to Shanghai, which was booming, to study
more Chinese. And I also had the chance
to travel more widely, including to
rural areas, many of which were
impoverished. I went to the Australian
National University, the ANU, to do a
PhD under the supervision of John Unger,
who's a leading expert on rural China.
John encouraged me to pursue my interest
in China's rural governance and rural
policies, which I did, ultimately
undertaking fieldwork in Yunnan in the
early 2000s. And Yunnan remains one of
my favorite parts of China. For the past
several years, I've been taking
undergraduate students to Yunnan to
experience and learn about rural China.
After graduating, I took up a position
at the ANU's Crawford School of Public
Policy,
and for the past 5 years, I've served as
the director of the Australian Centre on
China in the world, or CIW as we know
it, which was established by our former
Prime Minister Kevin Rudd and founding
director Jeremy Barme, to boost
Australia's understanding of China and
the Chinese world. And this book is very
much a product of our center's work.
We'll have to do another episode on
Yunnan. Just put that on your calendar
now. Sure. Great. Well, diving into your
latest volume,
to understand the CCP's durability, the
book looks at four key pillars of the
party's operations. Ideology and
discourse, organization, co-optation and
policy responsiveness, and coercion. And
I'm hoping to start with ideology. And
broadly, should we see the Communist
Party of China's ideology as a practical
or a cynical tool of governance and
control, or do you see party leaders as
authentically ideological people who are
pursuing some form of Marxism-Leninism
and Xi Jinping thought with genuine
conviction? Right. Well, as you pointed
out, the purpose of the book is to
provide a comprehensive understanding of
the reasons why the party has endured
through decades of remarkable social and
economic change.
Ideology is an important part of that
explanation, but not for reasons people
often assume. When we call a person or
an entity ideological, it's usually
disparaging. What we conjure with
ideological is the sense that people are
unbending, impractical, unreasonable,
that they're willing to make all kinds
of sacrifices, including to common
sense, to achieve a radical objective or
set of objectives.
And so when people refer to Communist
China, this conveys a sense that the CCP
is stubbornly committed to what many in
the West see as a failed project and/or
a highly undesirable means of organizing
society.
And I think most people in China would
agree that communism, at least in the
sense of communes and the centrally
planned economy, is undesirable. They'll
say, "We tried that and it didn't work.
It was a disaster." But
that's not to say ideology doesn't
matter to CCP leaders. It does matter,
but we need to understand where, when,
and how it matters.
The party is a Leninist organization
modeled on the Communist Party of the
Soviet Union. It's a party of
professional cadres whose job,
at least in theory, is to represent the
interests of the masses and whose job is
to lead the revolutionary struggle.
But the party has transformed itself
from a party that leads the workers and
peasants in class struggle into a party
whose mission is to lead all Chinese
people to national rejuvenation, to make
China great again. And Yijiang Bao's
chapter in that book really highlights
this transformation of a party of
workers and peasants into a nationalist
catch-all party, and he highlights this
as a key pillar of the party's
adaptability and durability.
Leninism also matters because it shapes
the way the party works internally.
Lenin's principle of democratic
centralism, for example, is a core
feature of the system. It values
internal debate and tolerates some
disagreement within the ranks, but once
a decision's taken at the top, everybody
is expected to fall in line behind the
leader. Leninism also shapes
state-society relations in China.
Political parties in the US, Australia,
and other competitive democracies seek
power over the constitutional order, the
state administration, essentially.
Leninism understands power more broadly,
for example, in economic structures and
social institutions. So, in its pursuit
of political power, the Leninist party
seeks to control those structures and
institutions, which is why the CCP has
its hands in everything.
Marx, of course, matters, too.
Marxist theory shapes the way the party
leaders see the world and perceive of
the challenges they face. I think the
prominent example here is Marxist theory
of historical materialism, the idea that
fundamental real-world contradictions
are the primary driver of social change.
In the Mao [snorts] era, the primary
contradiction
was defined as that between the
interests of the workers and the
interests of the owners of production,
the capitalists.
Now, the party under Xi defines the
principal contradiction
as that between inadequate, unbalanced
development and the people's need for a
better life.
So, Marxist thinking shapes policy. It
helps us to understand why the party has
moved away from growth at all costs to
embrace ideas such as ecological
civilization and common prosperity.
But it also highlights the flexibility
with which Marxism is reinterpreted and
applied to contemporary challenges. So,
Marxism matters, but it isn't dogmatic
and it doesn't limit the party's
options.
So, coming back to your question,
yes, I think that party leaders are
pursuing ideas with genuine conviction
and increasing confidence that they can
achieve their goals with existing
institutions and policy instruments,
but they're not ideological in the sense
of rigid dogma. They're practical-minded
and not constrained by ideology. And
they borrow heavily from outside ideas
when those ideas make sense, as the
chapter by Wendy Leutert and Sarah Eaton
in our book demonstrates. China wouldn't
be the powerhouse today if its leaders
consumed too much time by wondering
about how Marx or Lenin would respond to
the challenges they're facing. And so it
sounds like you're saying the party is
authentically ideological, but they use
ideology in ways that are intended
exclusively to enhance the authority and
the flexibility of the party rather than
constrain it in a more dogmatic way. Is
that fair? Yes, I think that's exactly
right. And what you often see, too, is a
reverse engineering, sometimes, of
practical policies or actions that the
party wants to take, and sometimes
they're initiatives to, among party
theorists and wordsmiths, to find the
right ideological framing which
demonstrates consistency and provides
the party with legitimacy and that
supports the continuity of its rule. And
how does Mao and Maoism fit into this?
What does Maoism really mean for today's
CCP and how has it enhanced the party's
durability? Well, yes, thank you
Henrietta and as you know, we have a
chapter on Mao and Maoism in the book
and
Mao matters
for a lot of reasons. First, he's the
founding father of the People's Republic
and the party is in power today because
of his political and military
achievements.
You can be critical of Mao in China
today, his actions, his policies and the
suffering he caused but you cannot
reject Mao.
To do so would be to reject the
foundation of CCP rule and the
justification for the party's continued
monopoly of political power.
To understand this, I think it's useful
to take a look at the party's official
historical narrative
and how this is communicated and taught
in China today.
The Maoist era is considered the period
in which China stood up,
threw off the shackles of imperialism
and entrenched CCP rule.
The Dengist period from the late '70s
through to Xi's ascension
is in the official narrative is
considered the period in which China
adjusted its ruling ideology and
policies to advance economic
development.
Now, the new era, the xin shidai, Xi's
era is the era in which China will
retake its rightful place as one of the
world's great nations. In this official
narrative, each of these periods builds
upon the former to propel China along
its path to national rejuvenation.
The Mao era does lay the necessary
foundations for the present era.
As for Maoism itself, many of Mao's
ideas remain influential in Chinese
politics today as Matt Galway describes
in his chapter. Again, not in a dogmatic
sense but in a strategic sense.
Mao's insights on political control, for
example, continue to shape party
thinking and policies. One example as
Matt highlights in his chapter is Xi's
anti-corruption campaign which in its
style, substance and practice has
antecedents in Mao's rectification
campaign in the early 1940s which
eliminated rivals, corrected ideological
thinking and strengthened Mao's personal
authority.
We had a great episode recently with
Minxin Pei who was arguing when it comes
to the purges of the Xi era that it
actually evoked for him more of a
Stalinist type of purge because Xi is
trying to use purges to control the
party rather than to overcome the party
as you might have construed Mao's
actions during the Cultural Revolution.
What would you think of that comparison?
Well, I admire Minxin Pei's work very
much but I'm not sure I entirely agree
that the Stalinist purges are a helpful
analogy. I think that, you know,
Stalin's extreme violence and murder
is not being mirrored today in China and
certainly there have been a huge number
of personnel changes but the idea of
purges sometimes evokes an extreme form
of violence in dealing with
political opposition or perhaps
political challenges or people who don't
meet with the leaders' expectations.
In China today, they're largely
administrative. I mean, certainly that
can end horribly for those who are the
targets of the reshuffling especially if
they're targeted in anti-corruption
campaigns. That is the end of careers,
possibly jail time but I don't think
that the extreme violence and murder and
mayhem of Stalin's purges is the best
analogy. I think again, there's
something different that's happening in
China and it's more sophisticated in its
operations.
So, I want to talk about linguistic
engineering which is a term that your
co-editor Fang Anqi uses in their piece
on discourse power in the book and she
argues that the party has very
successfully drawn on the same types of
what she calls linguistic engineering
that Chinese dynasties have actually
used for thousands of years to
legitimate their rule. So, what is
linguistic engineering in the Chinese
context and why is the party so good at
it?
Yes, indeed and this chapter in the book
also relates to the ideology pillar
and it's really important to understand.
Linguistic engineering is the systematic
effort to shape language in ways that
influence people's perceptions, values
and behavior.
In the Analects, Confucius said
that a ruler's first task is to rectify
names.
By which he meant that a ruler could
only successfully govern when there was
a shared understanding of reality, of
laws, of relationships and that this
required common language and
terminology.
Fang Anqi talks about this in her
chapter.
Confucian ideas were translated into
other formulations such as the five
relationships which reinforced social
and political hierarchies. Successive
Chinese emperors followed this principle
believing that the use of language
underpinned and necessarily underpinned
the social political order.
>> [sighs and snorts]
>> The CCP continued this tradition
adopting new terms and catchphrases to
support their political goals. Mao and
other CCP leaders adopted a suite of
slogans and terms in which party members
were trained
that shaped how people thought about
what was good and bad, right and wrong
in the new China. This was a time of
capitalist running dogs and evil gentry.
Most of the Maoist era slogans have now
been discarded
but the party continues to pay close
attention to language to bolster its
discourse powers
in ways that reinforce the continuity of
the political order.
In the early post-Mao years, party
leaders grappled with ways to represent
and communicate radical changes that
were getting underway. Socialism with
Chinese characteristics was one such
formulation which justified the adoption
of market reforms as being part of the
revolutionary project while perpetuating
the notion that China remained a
socialist country.
Deng also
resuscitated a Mao era maxim seek truth
from facts which communicated a move
away from Mao era ideological zealotry
toward a more pragmatic approach to
governing. And when Jiang Zemin came to
power, the party was in full transition
from a party of workers and peasants to
a nationalist party.
Jiang's slogan of the three represents,
sāngedàibiǎo,
sounds incomprehensible to many in its
English translation.
But it created a linguistic frame for
explaining why the party was embracing
entrepreneurs. That is, since the party
represented among other things China's
advanced productive forces,
entrepreneurs should thus be embraced by
the party.
>> [snorts]
>> Today, the party employs a wide range of
set phrases and expression known as tifa
to shape
political discourse and these include
core socialist values, common prosperity
and Chinese style modernization.
Some of these are more difficult to
comprehend than others
especially for English language
audience. One shiyer example is the two
must not negates, liǎngge bùnéngfoudìng,
which admonishes attempts to use the
reform era as a basis for criticizing
the Maoist era and vice versa.
This formula reinforces the notion that
there is a continuity in China's stages
of development from '49 to the present
>> [snorts]
>> and it communicates that the party has
known what it's doing all along.
Now, I should note that ordinary Chinese
citizens aren't using this formula in
everyday speech. In fact, many Chinese
citizens would have no clue what's meant
by the two must not negates
but the tifa shapes discourse in the
media and in the education system by
setting the ground rules for discussing
PRC the PRC and party history.
Effectively constraining the space in
which ordinary people would think about
the recent past in China even if they're
not thinking, I mean, maybe by design
not thinking about the explicit
parameters or the phrases themselves. Is
that fair? That's absolutely correct and
party leaders spend a lot of time
framing history and working on official
and correct versions of history and
making sure that those versions,
official versions of history,
predominate in the public discourse.
In fact, one of the several reasons it's
considered to be to have caused the
collapse of the Soviet Union
which is something that's studied very
closely
in among the Chinese leadership was that
the Communist Party of the Soviet Union
lost control of the official narrative
of its own history and the Communist
Party of China is determined not to make
the same mistake. So, the party is
increasingly, I think, relying on
nationalism and patriotism as
legitimizing
ideas for its rule and in her chapter in
the book, Dali L. Yang makes an
interesting angle on this issue on
patriotism, arguing that the power of
these ideas in China has emerged in
significant part from their
commodification
and their commercialization. So, what
does that look like? Sure. A key
ingredient of the party's ruling recipe
has been to find ways to mobilize the
citizenry behind its goals and its
leadership.
In the Maoist era, this manifested in
class struggle and the overthrow of the
old society.
Today, the party mobilizes people around
the China dream, the great rejuvenation
of the Chinese nation.
Nationalism has always been a powerful
force in CCP politics, but now it's
really front and center.
So, as Delia Lin's chapter explores, the
party mobilizes patriotism not only
through its own organs, propaganda,
media, education, but
by harnessing the market. The party has
embraced the market and consumerism, so
it only makes sense that patriotism
becomes a strategy for business, too.
Which again, I think highlights the
party's transformation, but also its
leaders' pragmatism.
Patriotic actions by entrepreneurs
are celebrated and rewarded, and one
obvious example is the film industry,
which gets access to serious funding to
produce positive representations of
China and party-led modernization.
It also manifests in the promotion of
Chinese brands, such as homegrown tech
products that are seen to rival the best
in the world. And one example, as I
think many of the your listeners will
know, was the Huawei Mate 60, the
production of which was widely
celebrated as a victory against US
sanctions.
That's a really interesting perspective.
So, turning to the next pillar of CCP
durability, you talk about organization.
So, how has the structure of the CCP
reinforced its longevity?
The party oversees an expansive and
really formidable administrative
apparatus that's been strengthened by
new rules, stronger oversight by party
functionaries, and tighter discipline.
The party recruits and promotes
increasingly well-educated officials and
invests much time and money in their
training.
Officials might not agree with
everything presented to them, and they
might tire of the study sessions,
but I think the net effect has been to
reinforce the notion that everyone's
part of on the same team
pursuing the party's sacred mission to
make China great again,
and that the party cadres, government
officials, should be prioritizing these
goals ahead of their private interests.
So, on that front, we can see that we
can say that she's been successful in
many of the reforms that he's brought to
state administration.
But I think it's always going to be a
work in progress, and it would be wrong
to characterize the party-state as one
in which the party center issues
directives and everyone else in the
system
simply obeys.
There are many bureaucratic interests to
navigate at every level in the system,
and players within the system know how
to advocate for their interests and to
find workarounds for directives they
find inconvenient.
But again, I would argue that this
represents a strength rather than a
weakness.
A country as vast as China
can't be easily governed from the
center, and local flexibility is a
necessity.
So, a big question in Chinese politics
and study of Chinese politics today is
whether tightened central controls have
gone too far, limiting the scope for
local innovation.
Nevertheless, I would argue that through
meritocratic recruitment and promotion,
party leaders have ensured that capable
people are running things at every
level, and that they understand what the
party's priorities are.
Next, we have co-optation, and you cite
the United Front Work Department as the
party's primary agent of co-optation.
So, why has the United Front been so
effective?
Well, first of all, I should say that
the party has a wide array of
institutional resources that support its
rule.
The United Front Work Department is a
somewhat of a unique institution
>> [snorts]
>> that seeks to ensure support for the
party and its policies among non-party
elites, including intellectuals,
religious, ethnic, and cultural elites,
entrepreneurs, too, and members of the
overseas Chinese diaspora.
So, the United Front Work Department has
been effective in co-opting people of
influence to prevent opposition, to
prevent political opposition, and to
make sure that important non-party
members of Chinese society and the wider
Chinese world are supportive or at least
not hostile to the party's agenda.
And it has a number of ways of doing
this. The United Front Work Department,
which has gained more resources and
absorbed other government agencies under
Xi,
is effective because it oversees a wide
variety of mechanisms for co-opting
people of influence, and these include
appointments to the eight minor
political parties
and to consultative bodies, which
provide access to officials and inputs
to the policy process.
So, even though entrepreneurs have now
been welcomed into the party as members,
the United Front Work Department also
recruits non-party entrepreneurs as
members of the All-China Chamber of
Commerce and Industry, which it
oversees, and which gives those
entrepreneurs a status, connections, and
an ostensible opportunity to provide
input into policy.
Xi, following Mao, has called the UFWD a
magic weapon. By magic, he means it's a
really efficient political tool.
Turning next to policy responsiveness,
the book asserts that the CCP,
notwithstanding its obvious
authoritarian character, can actually be
quite responsive to public opinion in
certain ways, and that this has also
reinforced its durability. So, what does
that look like in day-to-day governance?
Yes, this is an important part of the
story of the party's durability, and a
really important feature or pillar of
the party's success that's important to
understand. Party leaders, like
politicians everywhere, desire popular
approval for their work,
and a big part of the party's national
rejuvenation and modernization agenda is
improving livelihoods and making China a
better place to live.
The party's legitimacy has benefited
greatly from the livelihood improvements
of the reform era,
and as people's expectations change,
it's responding to them, too, with
better health care, clean streets, less
pollution, etc.
The party wants to keep China's growing
middle classes on side, and it thus has
to be responsive to their demands.
And of course, there's a lot of
literature on performance legitimacy in
authoritarian regimes in China
specifically, especially in the reform
era. But the [clears throat] Chinese
economy is slowing now, and there is
increasingly a discussion of a two-track
economy in which China is absolutely
generating impressive technological
innovations and
expanding its industrial capacity to
unprecedented scale, but ordinary people
are struggling to get by. It
increasingly feels like economic growth
is maybe not creating the a kind of
economy that people want to live in or
feel is getting better, at least, for
them. And so, in light of those trends,
do you expect this would undermine the
party's staying power in any meaningful
way, and how might the party try to
address the associated risks? Yes, the
economy is slowing, and resources in the
economy are concentrating in certain
sectors to the detriment of others,
and people everywhere, especially in
urban areas, are complaining about it.
The days of easy money and rapid upward
mobility are over.
But there's no sign that I see that this
is undermining the party's staying power
in any meaningful way,
not least because this is the system.
It's a system in which people live, and
there's no viable alternative. Sure, you
can opt out by emigrating if you have
the resources, but
for most people, the slowing economy is
simply where things are at right now,
and people are making the best of it. I
think it would take a much greater
economic shock to really shake people's
confidence in the system. Yeah. I mean,
we just saw the new five-year plan come
out recently at the Two Sessions, and it
seems like the party is adopting
incrementally more modest target for
economic growth, very limited agenda for
supporting consumption, and can direct
support to the population. So, in
thinking about, you know, policy
responsiveness as something that the
party has in some ways been quite good
at, like, how do you see the current
approach to China's economic challenges
is actually responsive in some way, or
is the party having more challenges
demonstrating responsiveness in this
complex economic environment?
Yes, I think there are two parts to that
question. One is how the party responds
to the broader challenges of the
economy, excessive investment,
overproduction, lack of consumption, and
there's certainly a lot of policy
rhetoric about that. But I think where
the rhetoric is focusing
away from growth at all costs towards
what the party refers to as high-quality
growth, I think this is signaling that
things are changing, things are going to
change. The China of double-digit growth
is in the past, and necessarily growth
has to slow down at a certain point. So,
partly it's recognizing the reality, but
it's also communicating in a lot of the
language that's used in the 5-year Plan
and in other policy documents that the
party is laser-focused on improving
people's quality of life, to addressing
inequality,
to providing better services, to taking
care of the environment, and to also
being incredibly successful in the
technologies, developing and supporting
the technologies of the future that are
going to make China great again, but
also to improve people's livelihoods.
So, the last pillar of the party's
durability that you cover in the book is
coercion. And of course, when the
party's gentler tools fail to prevent
opposition from emerging, it very
quickly turns to coercion. And so, can
you talk about the key components of how
the party thinks about coercion, and
also the stability maintenance system it
has built in China? Yeah, sure. So, if a
people or organization the party or
organizations the party deems a
political threat, the coercive apparatus
comes into play. And this apparatus is
vast both in terms of digital
surveillance of people's online
activity, and security personnel who
keep an eye on dissidents, human rights
lawyers, religious practitioners,
outspoken intellectuals, and other
potential troublemakers.
The police have a dedicated political
security unit, which manages networks of
informants.
And security personnel keep a close
watch on people who might challenge the
party's authority or cause embarrassment
by public protest. And such people are
kept under tighter surveillance during
sensitive periods such as the two
sessions that you just mentioned held in
March, when protests or unrest would
gain greater exposure and more
embarrassment to party leaders who prize
unity as a vital national strength.
In the book, we want to provide a
comprehensive picture of the pillars of
the party's staying power, and the
capacity to coerce is a core pillar.
But coercion is a means of last resort.
You mentioned when other gentler methods
fail.
And that's true. Coercion is expensive,
and it risks alienating people. But the
party will coerce when it needs to, and
it certainly has
formidable capabilities in that regard.
But I think it uses these tools much
less, I think, than many people in the
West, including policy makers, imagine.
And I think part of this is what you're
describing is because China, the party
has been able to create an environment
in which it can prevent behavior it
doesn't want to see before it happens.
And in the book, Anna Hayes in her
chapter writes a really interesting
piece on the party's near perfection of
what she calls preemptive policing. So,
how has this idea of preemptive policing
evolved, especially over the Xi era?
Yes, preemptive policing is the name of
the game these days, and the goal is of
course to nip problems in the bud before
they become a problem.
>> [snorts and gasps]
>> And I think this goes back to the shock
of the 1989 protests for the party
leadership. Since then, the party has
beefed up domestic security to ensure
that snowballing protests never happen
again. There is now a multi-layered
stability maintenance architecture
that Anna Hayes in her chapter talks
about, and it begins now with a grid
management system, which has been rolled
out over the past few years. And these
grids are divisions of approximately 3
to 400 households overseen by grid
managers, who are expected to report
problematic behavior or early signs of
conflict, and to intervene as necessary.
They and local government officials are
evaluated on how well they mediate
disputes and conflicts, and the mantra
is minor issues don't leave the village,
major issues don't leave the township or
town, and conflicts aren't escalated to
higher authorities. And this is a core
part of what's now widely promoted as
the Fengqiao experience, which is a
model of low-cost grassroots management.
The Fengqiao experience also is
including a sense that the community,
even outside of formal party structures,
has like a civic obligation to police
itself and kind of do the party's work
preemptively when it comes to
maintaining stability. That's right. I
mean, the grids themselves are
essentially civic organizations, even
though the assistants and attendants are
often remunerated, and some would argue
that's an extension of state
intervention into the local community.
But you're right, it certainly does
engage the community in this work, and I
guess that more than anything is what
the Fengqiao experience alludes to.
Interestingly, though, notwithstanding
all of this coercive power, explicit and
implicit, the party does sometimes allow
public protests to occur even now,
especially small-scale demonstrations on
local issues. And so, how does the party
think about what protests are acceptable
to them, and when they must be
eliminated? So, the party recognizes
that people occasionally need to let off
steam. And protests still take place in
China, but typically over local issues.
For example, protests against a dodgy
property developer who hasn't delivered
apartments on time, or in some cases
hasn't delivered them at all.
Protests against village leaders accused
of ripping people off in land deals, or
a factory that's polluting a local
waterway. And of course, there are labor
strikes, which are often about
nonpayment of salaries. But such
protests aren't seen as a political
threat if they target local entities,
and can be easily managed by local law
enforcement. And indeed, often local
authorities will take that as an
opportunity, take the opportunity to
help people to get restitution,
demonstrating their responsiveness.
Protests only become a threat when they
become translocal. That is, when people
with shared interests join forces
online, for example, or sympathy
protests break out in other areas, as
they've done in the case of ethnic
unrest.
So, if you're complaining about a local
problem, that's fine. If you start
joining forces with people to complain
about a national problem, then you're
going to get shut down, and ringleaders
will be punished. So, we've talked about
all these ways in which the party has
managed to stay in power for decades and
decades. But the party is not
invulnerable, and the book acknowledges
this, and you note that Xi's aggressive
centralization and personalization of
power has created new vulnerabilities.
And a leadership succession scenario,
for example, could very easily mire the
party in factionalism. And so, do you
see these vulnerabilities and others as
unique to Xi's particular model of
governance, and kind of the brittleness
that Xi's centralization of power has
created, or are these weaknesses
actually structurally predetermined?
Are these weaknesses the consequence of
the very same measures the party has
taken with great success so far since
1949 to remain in power?
Yes, succession is perhaps the biggest
challenge for the party, as it is for
all authoritarian governments. Xi's
personalization of power across the
political system and military won't be
easily replicated by new leader. For a
potential successor to aspire to such
lofty heights, Xi would really need to
be helping them get there already,
building the alliances and connections
and support that would be necessary for
such a strong future leadership role.
And we're not seeing that. We're not
seeing that. So, I think it's fairly
easy to draw a conclusion, even though
we are speculating about the future, but
I think most people would agree that
something very new will come after Xi.
Factionalism could return, and yes,
there could be a period of instability
as different interests within the system
pull in different directions. And the
book's final chapter by Richard McGregor
and Jude Blanchette explore these
different scenarios.
>> Jude Blanchette, importantly, former
host of this podcast. Indeed. Coming
back to your question, Henrietta, I
think this pattern is a structural
feature of the system. It's a system
which favors strong leaders through its
emphasis on unity, quick
decision-making, and of course, the
principle of democratic centralism.
Political authority flows from the top
down.
And in periods where there's no
paramount leader, centripetal forces
come into play until another strongman
brings them back together.
Well, then thank you so much for coming
on the show. Thank you, Henrietta. It's
been a real pleasure talking with you
and talking about our new book. To our
listeners, I do hope you'll be able to
read Anne's new compilation, The
Communist Party of China: Understanding
the Durability of the World's Most
Powerful Political Organization. It's a
really interesting read with a fantastic
range of authors. And as always, we
would love to hear what you thought of
today's conversation and what issues you
would like to see Pekingology unpack in
future episodes. You can send your ideas
to pekingology@csis.org.
And if you haven't already, please rate,

feed soon.

segments.text: China [music] is one of the 21st century's most consequential nations. It has never been more important to understand how the country [music] is governed and what its leaders and its people actually want and believe. Welcome to Pekingology, >> [music]

>> the podcast that unpacks China's evolving political system and the trajectory of China's domestic and foreign policy. I'm your host, Henrietta Levin, senior fellow with the Freeman Chair in China Studies at CSIS. [music] This is Pekingology.

I am so pleased to be joined today by Ben Hillman, director of the Australian Centre on China in the world at Australian National University and co-editor of a fantastic new book, The Communist Party of China, Understanding the durability of the

world's most powerful political organization. This volume tackles the question of why and how the CCP, the world's second longest ruling party anywhere, has been so successful at maintaining its own power. And the party's durability, I think is

all the more impressive when we think about the almost incomprehensible scale of change in China's economy and society since 1945. And yet here the party is maintaining a strong on on power through that whole duration and through a very

significant period of change. And so I'm really glad Ben is here to unpack the CCP's rather remarkable staying power. So, Ben, thank you so much for coming on the show. Thanks, Henrietta. It's a pleasure to be here and to be talking

about our new book, which I co-edited with my ANU colleague Feng Yuanji, and which is the culmination of many years' work by scholars in Australia and around the world. Well, we like to start all of our episodes with a question about how

our guest developed their interest in China and their expertise. So, what did that look like for you? Well, I first went to China in the early '90s and I spent time in the northeast, in Jilin province, studying Chinese initially.

And I was really struck at the time by the pace of change, the effervescent entrepreneurialism, and people's appetite for new ideas. In the northeast, which was a development laggard, I got insights into how people lived in Mao's era.

The people still lived in their work units and the friendship store was the only place to buy anything you needed. My teachers were retired literature professors who told me stories about life under Mao and the changes they'd

witnessed. And I really wanted to learn more. So, after finishing my bachelor's degree, I went back to China, this time to Shanghai, which was booming, to study more Chinese. And I also had the chance to travel more widely, including to

rural areas, many of which were impoverished. I went to the Australian National University, the ANU, to do a PhD under the supervision of John Unger, who's a leading expert on rural China. John encouraged me to pursue my interest

in China's rural governance and rural policies, which I did, ultimately undertaking fieldwork in Yunnan in the early 2000s. And Yunnan remains one of my favorite parts of China. For the past several years, I've been taking undergraduate students to Yunnan to

experience and learn about rural China. After graduating, I took up a position at the ANU's Crawford School of Public Policy, and for the past 5 years, I've served as the director of the Australian Centre on China in the world, or CIW as we know

it, which was established by our former Prime Minister Kevin Rudd and founding director Jeremy Barme, to boost Australia's understanding of China and the Chinese world. And this book is very much a product of our center's work.

We'll have to do another episode on Yunnan. Just put that on your calendar now. Sure. Great. Well, diving into your latest volume, to understand the CCP's durability, the book looks at four key pillars of the party's operations. Ideology and

discourse, organization, co-optation and policy responsiveness, and coercion. And I'm hoping to start with ideology. And broadly, should we see the Communist Party of China's ideology as a practical or a cynical tool of governance and

control, or do you see party leaders as authentically ideological people who are pursuing some form of Marxism-Leninism and Xi Jinping thought with genuine conviction? Right. Well, as you pointed out, the purpose of the book is to

provide a comprehensive understanding of the reasons why the party has endured through decades of remarkable social and economic change. Ideology is an important part of that explanation, but not for reasons people often assume. When we call a person or

an entity ideological, it's usually disparaging. What we conjure with ideological is the sense that people are unbending, impractical, unreasonable, that they're willing to make all kinds of sacrifices, including to common

sense, to achieve a radical objective or set of objectives. And so when people refer to Communist China, this conveys a sense that the CCP is stubbornly committed to what many in the West see as a failed project and/or a highly undesirable means of organizing

society. And I think most people in China would agree that communism, at least in the sense of communes and the centrally planned economy, is undesirable. They'll say, "We tried that and it didn't work. It was a disaster." But

that's not to say ideology doesn't matter to CCP leaders. It does matter, but we need to understand where, when, and how it matters. The party is a Leninist organization modeled on the Communist Party of the Soviet Union. It's a party of

professional cadres whose job, at least in theory, is to represent the interests of the masses and whose job is to lead the revolutionary struggle. But the party has transformed itself from a party that leads the workers and

peasants in class struggle into a party whose mission is to lead all Chinese people to national rejuvenation, to make China great again. And Yijiang Bao's chapter in that book really highlights this transformation of a party of

workers and peasants into a nationalist catch-all party, and he highlights this as a key pillar of the party's adaptability and durability. Leninism also matters because it shapes the way the party works internally. Lenin's principle of democratic

centralism, for example, is a core feature of the system. It values internal debate and tolerates some disagreement within the ranks, but once a decision's taken at the top, everybody is expected to fall in line behind the leader. Leninism also shapes

state-society relations in China. Political parties in the US, Australia, and other competitive democracies seek power over the constitutional order, the state administration, essentially. Leninism understands power more broadly,

for example, in economic structures and social institutions. So, in its pursuit of political power, the Leninist party seeks to control those structures and institutions, which is why the CCP has its hands in everything. Marx, of course, matters, too.

Marxist theory shapes the way the party leaders see the world and perceive of the challenges they face. I think the prominent example here is Marxist theory of historical materialism, the idea that fundamental real-world contradictions

are the primary driver of social change. In the Mao [snorts] era, the primary contradiction was defined as that between the interests of the workers and the interests of the owners of production, the capitalists. Now, the party under Xi defines the

principal contradiction as that between inadequate, unbalanced development and the people's need for a better life. So, Marxist thinking shapes policy. It helps us to understand why the party has moved away from growth at all costs to

embrace ideas such as ecological civilization and common prosperity. But it also highlights the flexibility with which Marxism is reinterpreted and applied to contemporary challenges. So, Marxism matters, but it isn't dogmatic and it doesn't limit the party's

options. So, coming back to your question, yes, I think that party leaders are pursuing ideas with genuine conviction and increasing confidence that they can achieve their goals with existing institutions and policy instruments,

but they're not ideological in the sense of rigid dogma. They're practical-minded and not constrained by ideology. And they borrow heavily from outside ideas when those ideas make sense, as the chapter by Wendy Leutert and Sarah Eaton

in our book demonstrates. China wouldn't be the powerhouse today if its leaders consumed too much time by wondering about how Marx or Lenin would respond to the challenges they're facing. And so it sounds like you're saying the party is

authentically ideological, but they use ideology in ways that are intended exclusively to enhance the authority and the flexibility of the party rather than constrain it in a more dogmatic way. Is that fair? Yes, I think that's exactly

right. And what you often see, too, is a reverse engineering, sometimes, of practical policies or actions that the party wants to take, and sometimes they're initiatives to, among party theorists and wordsmiths, to find the right ideological framing which

demonstrates consistency and provides the party with legitimacy and that supports the continuity of its rule. And how does Mao and Maoism fit into this? What does Maoism really mean for today's CCP and how has it enhanced the party's

durability? Well, yes, thank you Henrietta and as you know, we have a chapter on Mao and Maoism in the book and Mao matters for a lot of reasons. First, he's the founding father of the People's Republic and the party is in power today because

of his political and military achievements. You can be critical of Mao in China today, his actions, his policies and the suffering he caused but you cannot reject Mao. To do so would be to reject the foundation of CCP rule and the

justification for the party's continued monopoly of political power. To understand this, I think it's useful to take a look at the party's official historical narrative and how this is communicated and taught in China today.

The Maoist era is considered the period in which China stood up, threw off the shackles of imperialism and entrenched CCP rule. The Dengist period from the late '70s through to Xi's ascension is in the official narrative is considered the period in which China

adjusted its ruling ideology and policies to advance economic development. Now, the new era, the xin shidai, Xi's era is the era in which China will retake its rightful place as one of the world's great nations. In this official

narrative, each of these periods builds upon the former to propel China along its path to national rejuvenation. The Mao era does lay the necessary foundations for the present era. As for Maoism itself, many of Mao's ideas remain influential in Chinese

politics today as Matt Galway describes in his chapter. Again, not in a dogmatic sense but in a strategic sense. Mao's insights on political control, for example, continue to shape party thinking and policies. One example as

Matt highlights in his chapter is Xi's anti-corruption campaign which in its style, substance and practice has antecedents in Mao's rectification campaign in the early 1940s which eliminated rivals, corrected ideological

thinking and strengthened Mao's personal authority. We had a great episode recently with Minxin Pei who was arguing when it comes to the purges of the Xi era that it actually evoked for him more of a Stalinist type of purge because Xi is

trying to use purges to control the party rather than to overcome the party as you might have construed Mao's actions during the Cultural Revolution. What would you think of that comparison? Well, I admire Minxin Pei's work very

much but I'm not sure I entirely agree that the Stalinist purges are a helpful analogy. I think that, you know, Stalin's extreme violence and murder is not being mirrored today in China and certainly there have been a huge number

of personnel changes but the idea of purges sometimes evokes an extreme form of violence in dealing with political opposition or perhaps political challenges or people who don't meet with the leaders' expectations. In China today, they're largely

administrative. I mean, certainly that can end horribly for those who are the targets of the reshuffling especially if they're targeted in anti-corruption campaigns. That is the end of careers, possibly jail time but I don't think

that the extreme violence and murder and mayhem of Stalin's purges is the best analogy. I think again, there's something different that's happening in China and it's more sophisticated in its operations. So, I want to talk about linguistic

engineering which is a term that your co-editor Fang Anqi uses in their piece on discourse power in the book and she argues that the party has very successfully drawn on the same types of what she calls linguistic engineering

that Chinese dynasties have actually used for thousands of years to legitimate their rule. So, what is linguistic engineering in the Chinese context and why is the party so good at it? Yes, indeed and this chapter in the book

also relates to the ideology pillar and it's really important to understand. Linguistic engineering is the systematic effort to shape language in ways that influence people's perceptions, values and behavior. In the Analects, Confucius said

that a ruler's first task is to rectify names. By which he meant that a ruler could only successfully govern when there was a shared understanding of reality, of laws, of relationships and that this required common language and terminology.

Fang Anqi talks about this in her chapter. Confucian ideas were translated into other formulations such as the five relationships which reinforced social and political hierarchies. Successive Chinese emperors followed this principle

believing that the use of language underpinned and necessarily underpinned the social political order. >> [sighs and snorts] >> The CCP continued this tradition adopting new terms and catchphrases to support their political goals. Mao and

other CCP leaders adopted a suite of slogans and terms in which party members were trained that shaped how people thought about what was good and bad, right and wrong in the new China. This was a time of capitalist running dogs and evil gentry.

Most of the Maoist era slogans have now been discarded but the party continues to pay close attention to language to bolster its discourse powers in ways that reinforce the continuity of the political order. In the early post-Mao years, party

leaders grappled with ways to represent and communicate radical changes that were getting underway. Socialism with Chinese characteristics was one such formulation which justified the adoption of market reforms as being part of the

revolutionary project while perpetuating the notion that China remained a socialist country. Deng also resuscitated a Mao era maxim seek truth from facts which communicated a move away from Mao era ideological zealotry toward a more pragmatic approach to

governing. And when Jiang Zemin came to power, the party was in full transition from a party of workers and peasants to a nationalist party. Jiang's slogan of the three represents, sāngedàibiǎo, sounds incomprehensible to many in its English translation.

But it created a linguistic frame for explaining why the party was embracing entrepreneurs. That is, since the party represented among other things China's advanced productive forces, entrepreneurs should thus be embraced by the party. >> [snorts]

>> Today, the party employs a wide range of set phrases and expression known as tifa to shape political discourse and these include core socialist values, common prosperity and Chinese style modernization. Some of these are more difficult to

comprehend than others especially for English language audience. One shiyer example is the two must not negates, liǎngge bùnéngfoudìng, which admonishes attempts to use the reform era as a basis for criticizing the Maoist era and vice versa.

This formula reinforces the notion that there is a continuity in China's stages of development from '49 to the present >> [snorts] >> and it communicates that the party has known what it's doing all along. Now, I should note that ordinary Chinese

citizens aren't using this formula in everyday speech. In fact, many Chinese citizens would have no clue what's meant by the two must not negates but the tifa shapes discourse in the media and in the education system by setting the ground rules for discussing

PRC the PRC and party history. Effectively constraining the space in which ordinary people would think about the recent past in China even if they're not thinking, I mean, maybe by design not thinking about the explicit parameters or the phrases themselves. Is

that fair? That's absolutely correct and party leaders spend a lot of time framing history and working on official and correct versions of history and making sure that those versions, official versions of history, predominate in the public discourse.

In fact, one of the several reasons it's considered to be to have caused the collapse of the Soviet Union which is something that's studied very closely in among the Chinese leadership was that the Communist Party of the Soviet Union

lost control of the official narrative of its own history and the Communist Party of China is determined not to make the same mistake. So, the party is increasingly, I think, relying on nationalism and patriotism as legitimizing

ideas for its rule and in her chapter in the book, Dali L. Yang makes an interesting angle on this issue on patriotism, arguing that the power of these ideas in China has emerged in significant part from their commodification

and their commercialization. So, what does that look like? Sure. A key ingredient of the party's ruling recipe has been to find ways to mobilize the citizenry behind its goals and its leadership. In the Maoist era, this manifested in

class struggle and the overthrow of the old society. Today, the party mobilizes people around the China dream, the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Nationalism has always been a powerful force in CCP politics, but now it's really front and center.

So, as Delia Lin's chapter explores, the party mobilizes patriotism not only through its own organs, propaganda, media, education, but by harnessing the market. The party has embraced the market and consumerism, so it only makes sense that patriotism

becomes a strategy for business, too. Which again, I think highlights the party's transformation, but also its leaders' pragmatism. Patriotic actions by entrepreneurs are celebrated and rewarded, and one obvious example is the film industry,

which gets access to serious funding to produce positive representations of China and party-led modernization. It also manifests in the promotion of Chinese brands, such as homegrown tech products that are seen to rival the best

in the world. And one example, as I think many of the your listeners will know, was the Huawei Mate 60, the production of which was widely celebrated as a victory against US sanctions. That's a really interesting perspective.

So, turning to the next pillar of CCP durability, you talk about organization. So, how has the structure of the CCP reinforced its longevity? The party oversees an expansive and really formidable administrative apparatus that's been strengthened by

new rules, stronger oversight by party functionaries, and tighter discipline. The party recruits and promotes increasingly well-educated officials and invests much time and money in their training. Officials might not agree with

everything presented to them, and they might tire of the study sessions, but I think the net effect has been to reinforce the notion that everyone's part of on the same team pursuing the party's sacred mission to make China great again,

and that the party cadres, government officials, should be prioritizing these goals ahead of their private interests. So, on that front, we can see that we can say that she's been successful in many of the reforms that he's brought to state administration.

But I think it's always going to be a work in progress, and it would be wrong to characterize the party-state as one in which the party center issues directives and everyone else in the system simply obeys. There are many bureaucratic interests to

navigate at every level in the system, and players within the system know how to advocate for their interests and to find workarounds for directives they find inconvenient. But again, I would argue that this represents a strength rather than a weakness.

A country as vast as China can't be easily governed from the center, and local flexibility is a necessity. So, a big question in Chinese politics and study of Chinese politics today is whether tightened central controls have

gone too far, limiting the scope for local innovation. Nevertheless, I would argue that through meritocratic recruitment and promotion, party leaders have ensured that capable people are running things at every level, and that they understand what the

party's priorities are. Next, we have co-optation, and you cite the United Front Work Department as the party's primary agent of co-optation. So, why has the United Front been so effective? Well, first of all, I should say that the party has a wide array of

institutional resources that support its rule. The United Front Work Department is a somewhat of a unique institution >> [snorts] >> that seeks to ensure support for the party and its policies among non-party elites, including intellectuals,

religious, ethnic, and cultural elites, entrepreneurs, too, and members of the overseas Chinese diaspora. So, the United Front Work Department has been effective in co-opting people of influence to prevent opposition, to prevent political opposition, and to

make sure that important non-party members of Chinese society and the wider Chinese world are supportive or at least not hostile to the party's agenda. And it has a number of ways of doing this. The United Front Work Department,

which has gained more resources and absorbed other government agencies under Xi, is effective because it oversees a wide variety of mechanisms for co-opting people of influence, and these include appointments to the eight minor political parties

and to consultative bodies, which provide access to officials and inputs to the policy process. So, even though entrepreneurs have now been welcomed into the party as members, the United Front Work Department also recruits non-party entrepreneurs as

members of the All-China Chamber of Commerce and Industry, which it oversees, and which gives those entrepreneurs a status, connections, and an ostensible opportunity to provide input into policy. Xi, following Mao, has called the UFWD a

magic weapon. By magic, he means it's a really efficient political tool. Turning next to policy responsiveness, the book asserts that the CCP, notwithstanding its obvious authoritarian character, can actually be quite responsive to public opinion in

certain ways, and that this has also reinforced its durability. So, what does that look like in day-to-day governance? Yes, this is an important part of the story of the party's durability, and a really important feature or pillar of

the party's success that's important to understand. Party leaders, like politicians everywhere, desire popular approval for their work, and a big part of the party's national rejuvenation and modernization agenda is improving livelihoods and making China a

better place to live. The party's legitimacy has benefited greatly from the livelihood improvements of the reform era, and as people's expectations change, it's responding to them, too, with better health care, clean streets, less pollution, etc.

The party wants to keep China's growing middle classes on side, and it thus has to be responsive to their demands. And of course, there's a lot of literature on performance legitimacy in authoritarian regimes in China specifically, especially in the reform

era. But the [clears throat] Chinese economy is slowing now, and there is increasingly a discussion of a two-track economy in which China is absolutely generating impressive technological innovations and expanding its industrial capacity to

unprecedented scale, but ordinary people are struggling to get by. It increasingly feels like economic growth is maybe not creating the a kind of economy that people want to live in or feel is getting better, at least, for

them. And so, in light of those trends, do you expect this would undermine the party's staying power in any meaningful way, and how might the party try to address the associated risks? Yes, the economy is slowing, and resources in the

economy are concentrating in certain sectors to the detriment of others, and people everywhere, especially in urban areas, are complaining about it. The days of easy money and rapid upward mobility are over. But there's no sign that I see that this

is undermining the party's staying power in any meaningful way, not least because this is the system. It's a system in which people live, and there's no viable alternative. Sure, you can opt out by emigrating if you have the resources, but

for most people, the slowing economy is simply where things are at right now, and people are making the best of it. I think it would take a much greater economic shock to really shake people's confidence in the system. Yeah. I mean,

we just saw the new five-year plan come out recently at the Two Sessions, and it seems like the party is adopting incrementally more modest target for economic growth, very limited agenda for supporting consumption, and can direct

support to the population. So, in thinking about, you know, policy responsiveness as something that the party has in some ways been quite good at, like, how do you see the current approach to China's economic challenges is actually responsive in some way, or

is the party having more challenges demonstrating responsiveness in this complex economic environment? Yes, I think there are two parts to that question. One is how the party responds to the broader challenges of the economy, excessive investment,

overproduction, lack of consumption, and there's certainly a lot of policy rhetoric about that. But I think where the rhetoric is focusing away from growth at all costs towards what the party refers to as high-quality growth, I think this is signaling that

things are changing, things are going to change. The China of double-digit growth is in the past, and necessarily growth has to slow down at a certain point. So, partly it's recognizing the reality, but it's also communicating in a lot of the

language that's used in the 5-year Plan and in other policy documents that the party is laser-focused on improving people's quality of life, to addressing inequality, to providing better services, to taking care of the environment, and to also

being incredibly successful in the technologies, developing and supporting the technologies of the future that are going to make China great again, but also to improve people's livelihoods. So, the last pillar of the party's

durability that you cover in the book is coercion. And of course, when the party's gentler tools fail to prevent opposition from emerging, it very quickly turns to coercion. And so, can you talk about the key components of how

the party thinks about coercion, and also the stability maintenance system it has built in China? Yeah, sure. So, if a people or organization the party or organizations the party deems a political threat, the coercive apparatus

comes into play. And this apparatus is vast both in terms of digital surveillance of people's online activity, and security personnel who keep an eye on dissidents, human rights lawyers, religious practitioners, outspoken intellectuals, and other

potential troublemakers. The police have a dedicated political security unit, which manages networks of informants. And security personnel keep a close watch on people who might challenge the party's authority or cause embarrassment

by public protest. And such people are kept under tighter surveillance during sensitive periods such as the two sessions that you just mentioned held in March, when protests or unrest would gain greater exposure and more

embarrassment to party leaders who prize unity as a vital national strength. In the book, we want to provide a comprehensive picture of the pillars of the party's staying power, and the capacity to coerce is a core pillar.

But coercion is a means of last resort. You mentioned when other gentler methods fail. And that's true. Coercion is expensive, and it risks alienating people. But the party will coerce when it needs to, and it certainly has

formidable capabilities in that regard. But I think it uses these tools much less, I think, than many people in the West, including policy makers, imagine. And I think part of this is what you're describing is because China, the party

has been able to create an environment in which it can prevent behavior it doesn't want to see before it happens. And in the book, Anna Hayes in her chapter writes a really interesting piece on the party's near perfection of

what she calls preemptive policing. So, how has this idea of preemptive policing evolved, especially over the Xi era? Yes, preemptive policing is the name of the game these days, and the goal is of course to nip problems in the bud before

they become a problem. >> [snorts and gasps] >> And I think this goes back to the shock of the 1989 protests for the party leadership. Since then, the party has beefed up domestic security to ensure that snowballing protests never happen

again. There is now a multi-layered stability maintenance architecture that Anna Hayes in her chapter talks about, and it begins now with a grid management system, which has been rolled out over the past few years. And these

grids are divisions of approximately 3 to 400 households overseen by grid managers, who are expected to report problematic behavior or early signs of conflict, and to intervene as necessary. They and local government officials are

evaluated on how well they mediate disputes and conflicts, and the mantra is minor issues don't leave the village, major issues don't leave the township or town, and conflicts aren't escalated to higher authorities. And this is a core

part of what's now widely promoted as the Fengqiao experience, which is a model of low-cost grassroots management. The Fengqiao experience also is including a sense that the community, even outside of formal party structures,

has like a civic obligation to police itself and kind of do the party's work preemptively when it comes to maintaining stability. That's right. I mean, the grids themselves are essentially civic organizations, even though the assistants and attendants are

often remunerated, and some would argue that's an extension of state intervention into the local community. But you're right, it certainly does engage the community in this work, and I guess that more than anything is what the Fengqiao experience alludes to.

Interestingly, though, notwithstanding all of this coercive power, explicit and implicit, the party does sometimes allow public protests to occur even now, especially small-scale demonstrations on local issues. And so, how does the party
